items.prompt: What actually makes something an 'architectural style' rather than just a buzzword someone likes the sound of?
choices: Whether it appears in a lot of conference talks
It's a recurring shape that solves a recurring set of forces — chosen because a specific pressure (rule changes, team count, coupling cost) is expected to hurt
Whether it uses more services than the current design
Whether senior engineers approve of it
items.explanation: A style earns the name by being a repeatable answer to a repeatable problem. It becomes a buzzword the moment it's picked for its reputation instead of for a force actually present in the system being built.
items.reference:
🧱 Layered

call down through layers

⬡ Hexagonal

imports always point inward

📡 Event-driven

publish, don't call

🧩 Microservices

split the deploy unit

Why: each style is a bet about which axis of change (rules, integrations, team boundaries, deploy cadence) will hurt most.
items.learnMore:
Four recurring shapes
StyleOptimizesAccepts
LayeredSimplicityLeaky boundaries
HexagonalDomain independenceMore indirection
Event-drivenLoose coupling in timeEventual consistency
MicroservicesTeam/deploy independenceNetwork + ops overhead

None of the four is universally best — each is a deliberate bet made before the pain shows up, not a default.

Common mistake

Picking a style because its name sounds rigorous, without being able to finish the sentence "we're choosing this because our X is going to change, and this style protects against that."

items.prompt: Someone says 'we should use microservices' with no other explanation. Per L1, what test decides whether that's a real decision or a buzzword?
choices: Whether the team is excited about it
Whether they can finish the sentence 'we're choosing this because our X is going to change/grow, and this style protects against that'
Whether it's the newest style available
Whether a competitor uses it
items.explanation: L1's tell for a buzzword-driven choice is an unfinished sentence: no named force (team size, rule volatility, coupling cost) the style is actually meant to protect against. If the sentence can't be finished, the choice isn't grounded in the system's actual pressures.

items.prompt: In a plain layered (n-tier) architecture, what's the actual weak point of the style?
choices: It's always the slowest style to run
Nothing structurally stops a layer from reaching straight into a non-adjacent layer, or business rules leaking into the data-access layer
It requires more services than any other style
It can't be tested at all
items.explanation: Layered code is organized by convention, not by an enforced boundary — a controller can technically reach into the data layer, and business rules can end up embedded in a repository, unless the team actively disciplines the direction.
items.reference:
UI
↓
Business logic
↓
Data access

Why: cheapest to start and explain, but nothing structural stops a lower layer's details from leaking upward.
items.learnMore:
Layered (n-tier)

Code organized into horizontal layers, each calling only the one below it. The most familiar shape, and the cheapest to start.

Common mistake

Assuming the layers stay clean by default. Nothing in a plain layered app enforces the direction — business rules leak into the data layer unless someone actively guards against it.

items.prompt: What is layered (n-tier) architecture actually optimizing for, per L1?
choices: Independent deployability of each layer
The cheapest, easiest-to-explain starting shape — presentation, business logic, and data access, each calling the one below it
Isolating the domain from every framework
Eventual consistency between components
items.explanation: Layered is the default, low-ceremony shape: quick to start, easy to onboard a newcomer into. It doesn't buy domain isolation, deploy independence, or loose coupling in time — those are what the other three styles trade complexity for.

items.prompt: In hexagonal / clean architecture, which direction does the dependency arrow point?
choices: Outward — the domain imports whatever adapter it needs directly
Inward, always — adapters depend on the domain's port interfaces, the domain never imports an adapter
There's no enforced direction, same as layered
It varies per request
items.explanation: The defining rule of hexagonal architecture is that dependencies point toward the domain, never away from it. Adapters (DB, HTTP, queue) implement interfaces the domain defines; the domain itself has zero imports from any adapter.
items.reference:
Any adapter
→ (imports)
Domain core
✕ never imports back

Why: the dependency arrow always points inward, toward the domain, never out.
items.learnMore:
Hexagonal / clean architecture

The domain sits in the center, knowing nothing about databases, frameworks, or queues. External things plug in through ports the domain defines.

BuysCosts
Testable domain, no I/O neededMore files, more indirection
Swappable infrastructureA real learning curve

Common mistake

Calling a codebase 'hexagonal' because it has a folder named domain/, without the import direction actually being enforced anywhere.

items.prompt: What does hexagonal architecture buy that plain layered doesn't, per L1?
choices: Faster network calls
A domain that can be tested and reasoned about with zero real infrastructure, and swappable adapters, at the cost of more files and indirection
Independent deployability per layer
Guaranteed eventual consistency
items.explanation: Hexagonal's payoff is isolation: the business rule doesn't know or care whether it's backed by Postgres or an in-memory fake, so it's cheap to test and cheap to swap infrastructure. That isolation isn't free — it costs more files and a steeper first-read than a plain layered app.

items.prompt: What does an event-driven design buy, and what does it trade away, per L1?
choices: Buys nothing extra over layered; trades away readability
Buys loose coupling in time — a slow or down consumer doesn't block the producer — and trades away instant consistency plus easy single-stack-trace debugging
Buys guaranteed data consistency; trades away testability
Buys independent deployability of layers; trades away network reliability
items.explanation: Event-driven design decouples producer and consumer in time: the producer publishes and moves on. The cost is that a bug's trail is spread across a log of events rather than one call stack, and readers of the data may briefly see a stale or incomplete state.
items.reference:
📤 Producer publishes, returns immediately
📥 Consumer reacts later, independently

Why: a slow or down consumer no longer blocks the producer — that's coupling in time, removed.
items.learnMore:
Event-driven

Components communicate by publishing and reacting to events instead of calling each other directly.

Producer publishes OrderPriced
↓
Consumer reacts whenever it can

Common mistake

Treating 'loose coupling' as free. It's traded for eventual consistency and a debugging trail spread across an event log instead of one call stack.

items.prompt: A producer publishes an event and returns immediately, without waiting to know if the consumer succeeded. What is this style optimizing for?
choices: Fewer total lines of code
Decoupling in time — the producer's correctness stops depending on the consumer's uptime or speed
Guaranteeing the consumer runs before the producer returns
Removing the need for any data store
items.explanation: The whole mechanism exists to detach the producer's success from the consumer's availability — the producer no longer waits on, or is blocked by, a consumer that might be slow or down.

items.prompt: What specifically defines microservices as a style, beyond 'lots of small services'?
choices: Using more than one programming language
Independently deployable services, each with its own data store, typically owned by a separate team
Every function living in its own file
Using an event bus instead of REST
items.explanation: The defining property is independent deployability plus data ownership per service — not size, language count, or the transport mechanism used between them. A 'microservice' that shares a database with three others isn't really independent.
items.reference:
Service A
own deploy, own DB
Service B
own deploy, own DB

Why: the split is at the deployment level, not just the code level — each service ships on its own schedule.
items.learnMore:
Microservices

The system, not just the code, is split into independently deployable services, each owned by a team, each with its own data store.

Common mistake

Splitting a codebase into services while one person or team still owns all of them — that buys the network cost and none of the team-autonomy benefit.

items.prompt: A lone engineer working solo splits their small app into five microservices. Per L1's reasoning, what does this most likely buy them?
choices: Significant team-autonomy and deploy-independence benefits
Little to no benefit — the independence microservices buy comes from separate teams not blocking each other, which doesn't apply to one person coordinating with themselves
Automatic performance improvements
Guaranteed loose coupling in time
items.explanation: Microservices earn their operational cost (network calls, multiple pipelines, service discovery) by letting separate teams deploy independently. A solo engineer already has full coordination with themselves, so the split adds cost without the payoff.

items.prompt: Per L1, what's the first question worth asking before picking a style?
choices: Which style is trending in the industry right now
What's most likely to change here — the business rules, or the set of systems we talk to
How many GitHub stars each style's example repos have
Which style the last company the lead engineer worked at used
items.explanation: L1 opens the four-question list with what's most likely to change — rules favor layered/hexagonal, a shifting set of integrations favors event-driven. Trend-following and prior-company habit are exactly the buzzword-driven picks L1 warns against.
items.reference:
① What changes most: rules or integrations?
② How many people/teams touch this?
③ What does 'coupled' cost if we're wrong?
④ Can we afford eventual consistency?

Why: these four questions, asked before code, are what actually pick a style — not a preference for a name.
items.learnMore:

2How many teams?1 team → skip microservices
3Cost of being coupled and wrong?High → isolate the domain
4Afford eventual consistency?No → avoid pure event-driven for that path

Common mistake

Asking 'which style is best' instead of asking these four questions about the actual system in front of you.

items.prompt: Layered and hexagonal diagrams often look almost the same on a whiteboard. What's the real difference between them, per L2?
choices: Hexagonal always uses more services
The direction imports are allowed to point: layered has no enforced direction, hexagonal makes the domain importing an adapter structurally impossible
Layered is always faster at runtime
There's no real difference, only naming
items.explanation: The visible boxes-and-arrows can look identical; what differs is whether anything actually stops a lower/inner layer from importing an outer one. Hexagonal enforces the direction structurally — layered relies on discipline.
items.reference:
Layered: no enforced import direction
Hexagonal: domain never imports an adapter

Why: the difference lives in which direction an import is allowed to point, not in the folder names.
items.learnMore:
Same-looking diagrams, different rule

Layered and hexagonal can look nearly identical on a whiteboard. The actual difference is structural: hexagonal makes it impossible for the domain to import an adapter; layered just relies on nobody doing it.

Common mistake

Judging 'is this hexagonal' from a folder listing instead of from whether a lint rule over import direction would actually pass.

items.prompt: A team names a folder domain/ inside their layered app but nothing stops other layers from importing it in either direction. Is this hexagonal architecture?
choices: Yes, the folder name is what matters
No — hexagonal requires the dependency direction to actually be enforced, not just a folder labeled 'domain'
Yes, as long as the folder exists anywhere in the repo
It depends on how many files are inside the folder
items.explanation: A label without an enforced rule is cosmetic. Hexagonal architecture is defined by the direction dependencies are allowed to point — if imports can still flow either way, the naming doesn't change what the codebase actually is: layered.
items.reference:

Hexagonal: domain never imports an adapter

Why: the difference lives in which direction an import is allowed to point, not in the folder names.

choices: Having more than 100 lines of code
The domain module importing anything from a framework or adapter
The domain module being called by more than one adapter
The domain module having no unit tests
items.explanation: The pseudocode check is specific: a domain module fails if it imports a framework or adapter. It says nothing about size or how many callers it has — those aren't what the dependency rule is protecting.

items.prompt: Why does L2 restate the hexagonal dependency rule as pseudocode, instead of leaving it as a diagram?
choices: Diagrams are harder to draw than code
A pseudocode check is something that can actually be run over a codebase (e.g. as a lint rule) — a diagram can only be eyeballed
Pseudocode is required by the schema
It has nothing to do with enforcement, just clarity
items.explanation: The point of restating the rule as pseudocode is enforceability: a diagram is checked by eye and drifts unnoticed; a rule like `isHexagonal` can be wired into a linter and fail a build the moment a domain module imports an adapter.
items.reference:
if module is domain:
  return NOT imports adapter/framework
if module is adapter:
  return imports domain port

Why: this is a rule you can actually run over a codebase, not just eyeball on a diagram.
items.learnMore:
The dependency rule as a runnable check

L2's pseudocode turns 'is this hexagonal' from an opinion into something a lint rule can check: domain modules must not import adapters; adapters must import the domain's port interfaces.

Common mistake

Treating the dependency rule as a one-time design decision instead of something enforced on every PR — it erodes the moment someone imports a database client into a domain file 'just this once.'

items.prompt: If a linter rule modeled on L2's `isHexagonal` check would fail today on a team's 'domain' folder, what does that tell you?
choices: Nothing — the rule is only illustrative and not meaningful
The codebase isn't actually hexagonal regardless of what the folder is named, since the enforced direction is what defines the style
The team needs to rename the folder
The check is broken and should be ignored
items.explanation: The label on a folder is not the architecture. If a real dependency-direction check fails, the codebase doesn't have the property hexagonal architecture is named for, no matter what any folder is called.

items.prompt: In the pricing/loyalty sequence diagram from L2, what does the pricing service explicitly never learn about the loyalty handler?
choices: The customer's tier
Whether the loyalty handler succeeded, retried, or is behind — it publishes and moves on without waiting
The event bus's hostname
The total price of the order
items.explanation: That's the entire mechanism event-driven design relies on: the producer publishes and returns immediately, with no visibility into whether or when the consumer actually processes the event.
items.reference:
✅ Producer's correctness stops depending on consumer uptime
⚠️ Debugging shifts from a call stack to an event-log timeline

Why: loose coupling in time is a trade, not a pure win — it moves the debugging cost, it doesn't remove it.
items.learnMore:
What loose coupling in time actually costs

An event's producer never learns whether its consumer succeeded, retried, or is behind. That's the mechanism, not a bug — but it means 'did the side effect happen?' is no longer answerable from a single stack trace.

Common mistake

Treating event-driven as strictly better than a direct call. It trades one class of failure (blocking) for another (fragmented debugging, eventual consistency) — it doesn't eliminate failure.

items.prompt: Per L2, what does debugging shift to once a system becomes event-driven, compared to a direct synchronous call?
choices: Nothing changes about debugging
From reading a single call stack to reconstructing a timeline from an event log — a materially different skill and tooling investment
Debugging becomes strictly easier with no new tooling needed
Debugging becomes impossible entirely
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that this is a real shift, not a minor inconvenience: understanding what happened now requires reading and correlating an event log across services, rather than following one stack trace top to bottom.

items.prompt: Per L2, what makes a service boundary a 'good' one, as opposed to a bad one drawn through a shared concept?
choices: It has the fewest total lines of code on either side
It's drawn where the conversation between the two parts is already naturally rare and coarse, like one narrow event
It always matches the org chart exactly
It uses the newest available framework
items.explanation: L2's good-boundary example is pricing telling loyalty 'an order was priced,' once — a naturally infrequent, coarse-grained exchange. A bad boundary cuts through something both sides need constantly, like customer-tier lookups.
items.reference:
Good: one narrow, rare event
Bad: chatty back-and-forth over a shared concept

Why: a good service boundary is drawn where the conversation between two parts is already naturally rare and coarse.
items.learnMore:
Where to cut a service boundary

Splitting through a concept two parts both need constantly doesn't remove the coupling — it turns free function calls into network calls that carry the exact same coupling, plus latency and a new failure mode.

Common mistake

Drawing a service boundary along an org chart or a whiteboard's convenient dotted line, instead of along where the conversation between two parts is already naturally rare.

items.prompt: Two services need to constantly call each other for shared concepts like customer tier and order validity. What happens if you split them into separate microservices anyway?
choices: The coupling disappears because the code is now in separate repos
The exact same coupling remains, now as network calls instead of function calls, plus new latency and a new failure mode
Splitting always simplifies chatty relationships
Nothing changes at all
items.explanation: Splitting doesn't remove coupling that was never architectural in the first place — a chatty, shared-concept relationship stays chatty, it just becomes slower and more fragile because it now crosses a network.
items.reference:

Bad: chatty back-and-forth over a shared concept

items.prompt: Per L2, what does Conway's Law predict about a system's service boundaries?
choices: That services will always be perfectly independent regardless of team structure
That services tend to mirror the team's communication structure, whether that's planned or not
That microservices always outperform monoliths
That it only applies to companies larger than 500 engineers
items.explanation: Conway's Law is the observation that a system's structure tends to reflect the communication structure of the organization that built it — including when nobody intended that outcome.
items.reference:
🏢 Team communication structure ↔ 🧩 Service structure

Why: services tend to mirror the team's communication structure whether anyone plans it or not.
items.learnMore:
Conway's Law, applied

If pricing and loyalty logic are owned by the same two people, splitting them into two services buys two deploy pipelines to maintain and very little real independence — the same person still has to coordinate across both.

Common mistake

Splitting services before splitting the team's ownership — the service boundary can't buy independence the team structure doesn't already have.

items.prompt: If pricing and loyalty logic are both owned by the same two-person team, what does L2 say splitting them into two microservices actually buys?
choices: Full team-autonomy and deploy-independence benefits
Two deploy pipelines to maintain and very little independence, since the same people still coordinate across both
Automatic performance gains from having two processes
Nothing changes about who has to make cross-cutting changes
items.explanation: Independence has to already exist at the team level for a service split to realize it. Splitting a two-person team's code into two services adds pipelines and network calls without removing the coordination, because the same two people still own both.
items.reference:
🏢 Team communication structure ↔ 🧩 Service structure

Why: services tend to mirror the team's communication structure whether anyone plans it or not.
items.learnMore:

Common mistake

Splitting services before splitting the team's ownership — the service boundary can't buy independence the team structure doesn't already have.

items.prompt: In L2's decision flowchart, why does 'how many independent teams will touch this' come before 'is the boundary a rare, coarse conversation'?
choices: Alphabetical ordering of the questions
Team count decides whether splitting the deployment unit is worth considering at all — the boundary-quality question only matters once that's true
It doesn't matter which order they're asked in
Because team count is the easiest question to answer
items.explanation: If there's only one team, there's nothing to decouple by splitting into services — the boundary-quality question is moot. Team count gates whether the rest of the microservices branch of the flowchart is even relevant.
items.reference:
Team count first — it changes the cost of being wrong by an order of magnitude

Why: a bad layer boundary is a refactor; a bad service boundary is a multi-team migration.
items.learnMore:
Why team count goes first

L2's decision flowchart asks 'how many independent teams will touch this' before anything about event-driven or service boundaries — because that question determines whether splitting the deployment unit is even on the table.

Common mistake

Starting the decision procedure with 'which style sounds most rigorous' instead of with the question that changes the cost of being wrong the most.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does team count dominate the other three driving questions in practice?
choices: It's simply asked first in the list, with no other reason
It changes the cost of being wrong by an order of magnitude — a bad layer boundary is a refactor inside one repo, a bad service boundary is a multi-team migration
Because more teams always means more bugs
It doesn't dominate; all four questions are equally weighted
items.explanation: L2 is explicit about this: the stakes of a wrong call scale very differently. Fixing a layering mistake is a local refactor; fixing a wrong service boundary means coordinating a change across multiple teams and deploy pipelines.

items.prompt: Implement `makeEventBus()`: returns `{ publish(topic, payload), subscribe(topic, handler) }`. `subscribe` registers a handler for a topic; `publish` calls every handler registered for that topic with `payload`. Publishing a topic with no subscribers does nothing.

tests.expr: const bus = makeEventBus(); const seen = []; bus.subscribe('OrderPriced', e => seen.push(e.total)); bus.publish('OrderPriced', {total: 90}); expect(seen).toEqual([90])

tests.description: publishing with no subscribers does not throw

items.explanation: The bus is just a map from topic name to a list of handler functions; publishing walks that list and calls each one. Falling back to an empty array for an unknown topic is what makes publishing-with-no-subscribers a safe no-op instead of a crash.
items.reference:
The event-driven version publishes OrderPriced and returns — a minimal bus needs subscribe(topic, handler) and publish(topic, payload).

Why: this is the mechanism underneath 'the producer never waits on the consumer.'

items.explanation: Because handlers are stored in an array in subscription order and `publish` iterates that array in order, both `loyalty` and `analytics` fire on the same publish call, in the order they registered — exactly how L3's `loyaltyHandler` and a hypothetical `analyticsHandler` would both react to the same `OrderPriced` event.

items.prompt: The L3 edge cases warn that an at-least-once event bus can deliver `OrderPriced` twice. Implement `makeIdempotentHandler(fn)`: returns a wrapped handler that calls the real handler `fn(event)` the FIRST time a given `event.orderId` is seen, and does nothing on any repeat of the same `orderId`.

tests.expr: let count = 0; const h = makeIdempotentHandler(() => { count++; }); h({orderId: 'o1'}); expect(count).toBe(1)
let count = 0; const h = makeIdempotentHandler(() => { count++; }); h({orderId: 'o1'}); h({orderId: 'o1'}); expect(count).toBe(1)
let count = 0; const h = makeIdempotentHandler(() => { count++; }); h({orderId: 'o1'}); h({orderId: 'o2'}); expect(count).toBe(2)

items.explanation: A `Set` of already-processed order ids is enough: on each call, check membership before running the real handler, and record the id right before (not after) calling it so a duplicate delivered while the first call is still in flight is still caught.
items.reference:
L3's edge cases: an at-least-once event bus can redeliver OrderPriced — the consumer, not the bus, has to guard against double-processing.

Why: idempotency is what stops a redelivered event from awarding points twice.

tests.description: drops a duplicate orderId, keeps order

items.explanation: Walking the array once and tracking seen ids in a `Set` keeps the first occurrence of each `orderId` and drops every later duplicate, which is the batch-processing equivalent of `makeIdempotentHandler`'s per-event check.

items.prompt: Per L3's edge cases, what happens if event-driven code ships without any idempotency handling, and the event bus redelivers `OrderPriced` for the same order?
choices: Nothing — event buses never redeliver events
The loyalty handler may award points twice for the same order, unless it recognizes it has already processed that orderId
Checkout itself fails
The pricing service crashes on the second delivery
items.explanation: Most at-least-once buses will eventually redeliver a message. Without a check like `makeIdempotentHandler`'s, a handler with a side effect (awarding points) will simply run that side effect again for a duplicate delivery of the same event.
items.reference:
At-least-once delivery means a bus may redeliver the same OrderPriced event — the consumer has to dedupe by orderId, the bus won't do it for you.

Why: this is exactly the failure mode makeIdempotentHandler and dedupeOrderIds exist to prevent.

items.prompt: Per L3, whose responsibility is it to guard against a duplicate `OrderPriced` delivery — the event bus, or the consumer?
choices: The event bus — it guarantees exactly-once delivery by default
The consumer — the event contract has to carry enough information (like orderId) for the consumer to recognize and skip a repeat
Neither — duplicate delivery never actually happens in practice
The producer, by publishing the event only once ever
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that most buses are at-least-once, not exactly-once — so the consumer has to be the one that dedupes, using an identifier like `orderId` carried in the event payload, exactly what `makeIdempotentHandler` and `dedupeOrderIds` do.

items.prompt: Per L3's Version 4, what actually changes when `loyaltyHandler` moves from a module inside the same process (Version 3) into its own microservice?
choices: The event-passing code itself is rewritten from scratch

Nothing changes; it's purely a renaming exercise

items.explanation: L3 is explicit that Version 4's code inside each service looks almost identical to Version 3's publisher/handler pair. Why: microservices is event-driven's shape, taken one step further at the deployment level.
